extracted.intended_audience: manufacturers, merchants, political economists, and students of political economy
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and practical factors that determine commodity prices (momentary and long-run), including verification costs, durability, supply concentration, speculation, and measurement issues for comparing prices across time and places.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost of verification (verification on price)
rubrics_metrics.description: The momentary amount of price depends upon the proportion existing between supply and demand, and also upon the cost of verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When buyers cannot readily verify quality (as in flax, lace, watches, drugs, or linen widths), sellers can obtain higher prices by fraud or concealment; purchasers often must pay for a third party's skill and integrity to ascertain quality. Examples given: damped/flawed flax packed with stones; 'single-press' vs 'double-press' lace indistinguishable without magnifying-glass; stockings stretched and retaining a baggy shape after washing; forged watch marks; apothecaries' medicines where adulteration is hard to detect. Result: verification costs raise the effective price and create market inefficiencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraud and adulteration damage trade reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: The manufacture and sale of fraudulent or inferior articles can decimate demand and ruin the credit of an entire locality's product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee evidence: 'all the witnesses attribute the decay of the trade more to the making of fraudulent and bad articles, than to the war, or to any other cause.' Examples: Nottingham lace losing orders where fraud discovered; watch exports depressed by poorly made but showy watches. Anti-pattern: widespread cheap, showy but nonfunctional products undermine entire markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supply concentration and monopoly effects on momentary price
rubrics_metrics.description: If the whole supply (or present stock) of a commodity is in the possession of one person he will set a price to maximize money realized, guided by expected diminished consumption and by timing before new supply arrives; if several dealers hold the stock, immediate competition alters pricing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish single-holder pricing behavior from multiple-dealer competition; consider holders' differing views on duration of supply shortage and their capital circumstances. This principle underlies speculations and stock-holding strategies to influence prices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perishability limits monopoly pricing
rubrics_metrics.description: If a commodity is perishable, time supplies the place of competition and it will scarcely reach a monopoly price even if held by few persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a cargo of ice imported to London; perishability means goods must be sold before spoilage, preventing sustained monopoly pricing. Apply when assessing whether stockpiling can raise price.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speculation and stockholding can cause price spikes
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent speculations are often founded on purchasing all stock on hand and agreeing for expected arrivals, with the aim of procuring a larger average price by holding stock in few hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by cajeput oil in 1831 where limited holders and active trading pushed prices from 7d. per ounce to many shillings within months. Recognize the mechanism: concentrated holdings + trading frequency + expectations about arrivals produce rapid price changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Durability influences permanent average price
rubrics_metrics.description: The durability of any commodity influences its cost in a permanent manner: what is consumed in use must at minimum fetch the labour cost of production, whereas articles that do not wear out may have prices permanently below production cost until renewed demand triggers production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: consumables (matches, food, cigars) cannot sustainably sell below production labour cost; durable goods (well-cut precious stones) retain value and can be resold at similar per-unit prices; long-lived manufactured goods can depress long-run prices because existing stock persists. Consider resale markets and second-hand channels when evaluating long-run price effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms of obsolescence
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles become 'old' from (1) actual decay or wearing out of parts, (2) improved modes of construction, or (3) changes in form and fashion required by taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the latter two cases utility may be little diminished but demand shifts to other social classes, producing second-hand markets and downward propagation of luxury tastes. Example: looking-glasses can be cut into smaller usable pieces when cracked; fashion and construction improvements create markets for formerly costly goods among less affluent classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Money price is an unreliable cross-time/cross-country measure
rubrics_metrics.description: The money price furnishes comparatively little information when comparing distant intervals of time or different countries because gold and silver (money) are themselves subject to variation; there is no invariable standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: consider using a day's labour of an agricultural labourer (Malthus' proposal) as a comparative unit, possibly combined with other common trades requiring moderate skill (blacksmith, carpenter). Also consider how many days' labour wages purchase of staple food for deeper comparisons. Use care when comparing nominal money prices across eras or regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect empirical averages and deviations from merchants/manufacturers
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturers and merchants should collect averages from actual sales recorded in their books, including quantities and greatest deviations from the mean, to provide valuable factual data for political economists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggestion: a small committee could collate averages from many quarters; such data (with sample sizes and variability) would improve economic inference and correct overreliance on theory where facts are scarce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major causes of long-term price diminution
rubrics_metrics.description: Several causes may produce a long-term diminution in the price of manufactured articles: (1) alteration in the value of the currency; (2) increased value of gold from increased demand for coin; (3) diminished rate of profit produced by capital; (4) diminished price of raw materials; (5) smaller quantity of raw material employed or inferior workmanship; (6) improved means of producing the same effect with diminished labour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing historical price declines, estimate the relative contribution of each cause (e.g., compare gold price, interest rates/3% consol prices, raw material prices, and technological changes). Use tables and empirical data to disentangle effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Middlemen can be advantageous or add unnecessary cost
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of a class of middle-men between small producers and merchants is frequently advantageous to both parties, but when numerous they may enhance the price without equivalent good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: London 'brass-plate coal-merchants' supply five-sixths of London through intermediaries who take commissions and increase consumer cost. Evaluate whether middlemen add services (wharfs, logistics) or merely extract commissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raw material versus labour composition of value
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the cost of any article may be reduced in ultimate analysis to the quantity of labour by which it was produced, in practice many products are treated as 'raw materials' at intermediate stages where only moderate labour has been expended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace proportions in which raw material and labour unite to constitute value (e.g., iron as raw material for tools). Use this decomposition when assessing how changes in raw-material prices or labour-saving techniques affect final prices.
